title: CVE-2025-13281: Portworx Half-Blind SSRF in kube-controller-manager
need_summary: Whether CVE-2025-13281 in kube-controller-manager is fixed and what versions/PRs closed the half-blind SSRF in the in-tree Portworx StorageClass, anchored on the listed fixed versions and PRs #135081/#135193/#135192/#135191.
security_topic: mitigation and fixed versions for Portworx SSRF in kube-controller-manager
question_text: ### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?
answer_text:
This issue can be mitigated by upgrading to a fixed kube-controller-manager version or by enabling the CSIMigrationPortworx feature gate (if it was overridden from its default value in versions greater than equal to v1.31).

#### Fixed Versions
- kube-controller-manager: >= v1.32.10
- kube-controller-manager: >= v1.33.6
- kube-controller-manager: >= v1.34.2
thread_text:
ISSUE #135525: CVE-2025-13281: Portworx Half-Blind SSRF in kube-controller-manager
Author: natherz97
Date: 2025-11-30T23:08:37Z
Labels: kind/bug, area/security, committee/security-response, needs-triage, official-cve-feed
State: closed

[c0]
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3-1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:N/A:N) - Medium (5.8)

A half-blind Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability exists in kube-controller-manager when using the in-tree Portworx StorageClass. This was patched for other in-tree StorageClasses (GlusterFS, Quobyte, StorageOS, and ScaleIO) as part of[ CVE-2020-8555](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91542). This vulnerability allows authorized users to leak arbitrary information from unprotected endpoints in the control plane’s host network (including link-local or loopback services). 

An attacker with permissions to create a pod using the built-in Portworx StorageClass can cause kube-controller-manager to make GET requests (without an attacker controlled request body) from within the control plane’s host network and make the corresponding HTTP response body visible as part of event objects created by kube-controller-manager.

The in-tree Portworx StorageClass has been disabled by default starting in version v1.31 from the CSIMigrationPortworx feature gate. As a result, currently supported versions greater than or equal to v1.32 are not impacted unless the CSIMigrationPortworx feature gate is disabled with an override.

### Am I vulnerable?

You may be vulnerable if all of the following are true:
- You are running a vulnerable version and have manually disabled the CSIMigrationPortworx feature gate.
- There are unprotected endpoints normally only visible from the control plane’s host network (including link-local metadata endpoints, unauthenticated services listening on localhost, or other services in the control plane’s private network).

A half-blind Server Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability exists in kube-controller-manager when using the in-tree Portworx StorageClass. This was patched for other in-tree StorageClasses (GlusterFS, Quobyte, StorageOS, and ScaleIO) as part of[ CVE-2020-8555](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91542). This vulnerability allows authorized users to leak arbitrary information from unprotected endpoints in the control plane’s host network (including link-local or loopback services).

### What happened?

DRA extended resource quota getVerifiedPodUsage has a loophole that would allow any number of resourceclaims saying they were owned by the same pod and setting the same annotation to skip getting counted by quota

a user cannot work around the system admin created quota to request DRA extended resource devices

so a user could

2) make any number of resourceclaims pretending to be extended resource claims for that pod and skip getting counted by quota
3) make other pods using their resource claims

title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy namespace lookup raced newly created namespaces, produces spurious "namespace not found" rejections
need_summary: Whether the namespace-lookup race in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy could wrongly reject requests, and the maintainer points to the fix in Kubernetes PR 135359.
security_topic: namespace lookup fallback missing in ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
question_text:
When creating new workload (observed with Deployment and StatefulSet) immediately after creating its namespace, there is a possibility that watch case has not yet caught up to the new namespace existing.

Naively, this would result in frequent failures, but apiserver guards against this by falling back to live client when namespace was `NotFound`. Example: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ab3e83f73424a18f298a0050440af92d2d7c4720/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/admission/plugin/webhook/predicates/namespace/matcher.go#L88

The issue happens infrequently but can be forced by overriding informer lister to always return NotFound for a specific namespace (see repro instructions below). This way, the call to informer's lister would always fail, while the call to client would remain unaffected - this would force the fallback path, ensuring it is present.

### What did you expect to happen?

No 404 errors when creating StatefulSets in existing namespaces - even immediately after ns creation.
answer_text:
It looks like it's the namespace lookup done as part of ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, which didn't have the live lookup fallback.

Fix in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135359

Nothing changed related to this in 1.32 → 1.33 ... I suspect you just saw ValidatingAdmissionPolicies added to your cluster in that upgrade that started hitting this.

### What happened?

When creating new workload (observed with Deployment and StatefulSet) immediately after creating its namespace, there is a possibility that watch case has not yet caught up to the new namespace existing.

Naively, this would result in frequent failures, but apiserver guards against this by falling back to live client when namespace was `NotFound`. The issue happens infrequently but can be forced by overriding informer lister to always return NotFound for a specific namespace (see repro instructions below). This way, the call to informer's lister would always fail, while the call to client would remain unaffected - this would force the fallback path, ensuring it is present.

### What did you expect to happen?

No 404 errors when creating StatefulSets in existing namespaces - even immediately after ns creation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?



```
--- a/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/listers/core/v1/namespace.go
+++ b/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/listers/core/v1/namespace.go
@@ -20,7 +20,6 @@ package v1

 import (
        corev1 "k8s.io/api/core/v1"
-       errors "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/api/errors"
        labels "k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/labels"
        listers "k8s.io/client-go/listers"
        cache "k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache"
@@ -47,17 +46,3 @@ type namespaceLister struct {
 func NewNamespaceLister(indexer cache.Indexer) NamespaceLister {
        return &namespaceLister{listers.New[*corev1.Namespace](indexer, corev1.Resource("namespace"))}
 }
-
-// Get retrieves the Namespace from the index for a given name.
-// Objects returned here must be treated as read-only.
-// This method overrides the embedded Get to add custom logic.
-func (nl *namespaceLister) Get(name string) (*corev1.Namespace, error) {
-       // 1. Check if the requested namespace is "lalala"
-       if name == "lalala" {
-               // 2. Return not found error if it is
-               return nil, errors.NewNotFound(corev1.Resource("namespace"), name)
-       }
-       // 3. Otherwise, use the parent implementation from the embedded ResourceIndexer
-       return nl.ResourceIndexer.Get(name)
-}
-
```


Steps to reproduce:

  1. Apply the diff above to apiserver code.
  2. Set up a cluster using that apiserver.
  3. Create the namespace "lalala"
  4. Create a StatefulSet in that namespace
  5. Observe the request failing with 404 - it should succeed despite the damaged lister code

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

Based on our (limited) set of observations, we believe the regression happened between 1.32 and 1.33

Observations were made in GKE

title: Creating a Service without Name creates an invalid IPAddress
need_summary: Whether creating a Kubernetes Service without a name can trigger an apiserver denial-of-service due to repeated invalid IPAddress allocation, as shown in the issue discussion and the repro/timeout logs.
security_topic: apiserver denial-of-service from invalid Service creation
question_text:
When creating k8s Service without name it tries to create an invalid IPAddress.

Author: aojea

When creating k8s Service without name it tries to create an invalid IPAddress.

This is because the Service apiserver registry tries to allocate the ClusterIP, if not set, before the object name has been validated.

We could/should validate that the IPAddress object we are going to be create is correct, and fail fast avoiding the penalty of failing an API request, something like

+       // obtain the Parent Reference, since IPAddress is generated before the Service object is created,
+       // the Service reference can be nil and fail later during the creation of the IPAddress object.

@@ -148,10 +155,10 @@ func (a *Allocator) createIPAddress(name string, svc *api.Service, scope string)

title: [NodeDeclaredFeatures] GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize version skew problem
need_summary: Whether the NodeDeclaredFeatures change wrongly blocks previously allowed guaranteed pod CPU resizes, and the issue was resolved by removing the declared feature in Kubernetes PR 136759.
security_topic: version-skew regression in node-declared features for pod CPU resize
question_text:
The `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` node declared feature isn't just tied to the `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature gate: it declares the feature if the feature gate is enabled OR the node doesn't use static CPU policy, and then requires the feature gate for all CPU resizes of guaranteed pods.

Here is the problem:
- v1.34 node: in-place pod resize is enabled, static policy disabled
	- 1.34 is pre-NDF, so it doesn't declare any features
- v1.35 control plane: NDF disabled (still alpha)
	- resizing guaranteed pod CPU is allowed (no NDF admission check), node doesn't mark resize as infeasible since it doesn't have static CPU policy.
- Upgrade cluster to v1.36: NDF goes beta & default enabled
	- Now resizing a guaranteed pod's CPU requires the `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize`, but the v1.34 node still doesn't set it, causing a regression.

I don't think we need to fix this in v1.35 since NDF is still alpha, but this is a beta-blocker.

/assign @pravk03 
/cc @natasha41575 
/milestone v1.36
answer_text: The declared feature was removed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/136759, so I think we can close this now.
thread_text:
ISSUE #135329: [NodeDeclaredFeatures] GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize version skew problem
Author: tallclair
Date: 2025-11-17T19:18:04Z
Labels: sig/node, triage/accepted
State: closed

[c0]
The `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` node declared feature isn't just tied to the `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature gate: it declares the feature if the feature gate is enabled OR the node doesn't use static CPU policy, and then requires the feature gate for all CPU resizes of guaranteed pods.

Here is the problem:
- v1.34 node: in-place pod resize is enabled, static policy disabled
	- 1.34 is pre-NDF, so it doesn't declare any features
- v1.35 control plane: NDF disabled (still alpha)
	- resizing guaranteed pod CPU is allowed (no NDF admission check), node doesn't mark resize as infeasible since it doesn't have static CPU policy.
- Upgrade cluster to v1.36: NDF goes beta & default enabled
	- Now resizing a guaranteed pod's CPU requires the `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize`, but the v1.34 node still doesn't set it, causing a regression.

I don't think we need to fix this in v1.35 since NDF is still alpha, but this is a beta-blocker.

/assign @pravk03 
/cc @natasha41575 
/milestone v1.36

--- COMMENTS ---
[c1] @natasha41575 2025-11-17T19:57:16Z:
An idea I was toying around with when thinking about the other resize feasibility checks was inverting the logic: instead of the resize requiring a node declared feature to be set, the resize could be rejected if a feature is set.

In this case:
- Surface the node declared feature `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUsDisabled` (or whatever name) if the node uses static CPU policy AND the feature gate is disabled
- During admission, *reject* the resize if the node declared feature `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUsDisabled` is set

That way:
- ~with 1.36 control plane and 1.34 kubelet: the node declared feature will not be set, the patch will be permitted, and the 1.34 kubelet would run its feasibility checks (which would reject the resize as Infeasible)~
- with 1.36 control plane and 1.36 kubelet: the node declared feature *will* be set, and the patch will be rejected. 

Just my two cents!

ETA: Synced with Praveen offline, and have come to the understanding that ideally we would not rely on the kubelet checks in the old node, which makes sense.
---
[c2] @pravk03 2025-11-17T19:57:59Z:
This is an issue with `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` because it depends on both feature gate and node config and NDF is not GA. If the declared feature relied solely on the feature gate (like [InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d450ef773127374148abad4daaf28dac6cb2625/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/nodedeclaredfeatures/features/inplacepodresize/pod_level_resource_resize.go)), this is not a problem. 
---
[c3] @pravk03 2025-11-17T20:10:01Z:
> Surface the node declared feature InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs (or whatever name) if the node uses static CPU policy AND the feature gate is disabled

I think we would still run into the same issue as `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature graduates to Beta/GA.  I do not think its a good idea to have declared features based on inverse of feature gates.  
---
[c4] @AadiDev005 2025-11-19T17:37:07Z:
It looks like the core challenge is the inconsistent behavior caused by the interplay of feature gates and node-declared features (NDF), especially across different Kubernetes versions.

One rough idea I’m considering is the concept of inverting the logic for the node declared feature: instead of requiring the feature to be set to allow resize, we reject the resize if an "exclusive CPUs disabled" feature is set on the node. This could help handle older nodes and avoid relying solely on kubelet checks in legacy versions.

I’d love to get feedback on this approach or any alternative ideas you think might make sense before digging deeper.

---
[c5] @tallclair 2025-11-20T19:23:39Z:
@AadiDev005 was that an AI generated comment? It looks like you're just paraphrasing earlier comments and presenting the ideas as your own 😞 
---
[c6] @tallclair 2025-11-20T19:32:55Z:
I think as it is, NodeDeclaredFeatures (NDF) doesn't match this use case. The problem stems from the fact that at the API level we're tightening the restrictions, by forbidding something that used to be allowed (resizing guaranteed pod CPU). This mostly stems from the fact that NDF didn't exist when we first introduced the feature gate for static CPU resize. If we had this feature gate from the beginning, it wouldn't have been an issue.

I think @natasha41575's suggestion to invert the logic, to have "Forbidden Features" rather than "Required Features" could be used for this, but I'm not sure we want to go that route. It's sort of weird for nodes to start advertising that they don't support a feature, since that implies that any node not advertising the negative feature DOES support it? Can we ever remove it in that case? Maybe this would be useful functionality to have for deprecations?
---
[c7] @pravk03 2025-11-20T20:29:32Z:
Would it be acceptable to tighten the restrictions with NDF if there are existing Kubelet validations for the same feature ?. Specifically in the case of `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize`, the Kubelet currently marks resize requests with static policy as infeasible on nodes without NDF ([here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5bcb7599736327cd8c6d23e398002354a6e40f68/pkg/kubelet/allocation/allocation_manager.go#L693)), whereas on nodes with NDF, we reject the request during admission. While this admission behavior is inconsistent, it should resolve once NDF is enabled on all nodes. From the Pod's perspective, the net effect with and without NDF is the same ?
---
[c8] @tallclair 2025-11-21T17:31:43Z:
Yeah, I think that's OK. In that case, we're just shifting the error to surface earlier. The problem we encountered in this issue is that pods that _wouldn't_ be marked infeasible can be rejected.
---
[c9] @natasha41575 2026-01-14T22:35:44Z:
> This mostly stems from the fact that NDF didn't exist when we first introduced the feature gate for static CPU resize.

I wonder if we should just state that NDF can't be used retroactively to block admission requests that would have previously succeeded. Net-new features (like PLR + IPPR) can make use of NDF if they are baked into the initial implementation/design, but otherwise it doesn't seem to fit the use case. 

This would make NDF useless for moving IPPR feasibility checks ... originally I was hoping it could be useful for `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize`, an analogous `GuaranteedQoSPodMemoryResize`, and maybe even resize + swap. But maybe not...
---
[c10] @pravk03 2026-02-04T01:11:55Z:
(Capturing discussions from slack and meetings)

The main concern here is that admission selectively depends on a feature gate, and NDF does not work well in such cases. 

Currently, `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` is declared by the node when the below conditions are met 
- `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature gate is enabled and Atatic CPU policy is enabled
**OR**
- Static CPU policy is disabled (feature gate is irrelevant here).

Since new declared features are not added on older nodes, requests that were previously allowed - specifically when the feature gate is irrelevant, would start to fail after the declared feature is added.

Based on the discussions, its better to stop declaring features that selectively depend on feature gates. I will make a change to stop declaring [GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1861c1a07244e8e9430aaf588722dd22287c471e/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/nodedeclaredfeatures/features/inplacepodresize/guaranteed_cpu_resize.go)
---
[c11] @SergeyKanzhelev 2026-02-06T17:52:37Z:
> Based on the discussions, its better to stop declaring features that selectively depend on feature gates. I will make a change to stop declaring [GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1861c1a07244e8e9430aaf588722dd22287c471e/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/nodedeclaredfeatures/features/inplacepodresize/guaranteed_cpu_resize.go)

what kind of feedback does this gives us? What would be the "correct" way of using NDF in cases like this going forward?
---
[c12] @natasha41575 2026-02-06T18:30:05Z:
> > Based on the discussions, its better to stop declaring features that selectively depend on feature gates. I will make a change to stop declaring [GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1861c1a07244e8e9430aaf588722dd22287c471e/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/nodedeclaredfeatures/features/inplacepodresize/guaranteed_cpu_resize.go)
> 
> what kind of feedback does this gives us? What would be the "correct" way of using NDF in cases like this going forward?

If there is a net-new feature, I think NDF can be used for these cases. The problem is that IPPR was implemented pre-NDF.

Say we had NDF at the time that IPPR was being implemented and we had used it. Version N control plane would selectively block admission requests where `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` FG was not present. This is okay, because N-3 nodes would not have permitted IPPR at all, because it was not a supported feature. 

The problem is that we are trying to introduce NDF _after_ IPPR is GA. Version N control plane is blocking admission requests where `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` FG is not present. But this is _not_ okay, because N-3 nodes do support IPPR, and we do not want control plane to block the request in all cases. 

For these cases, I think it just means that we have to wait for NDF to be GA+3.



---
[c13] @SergeyKanzhelev 2026-02-06T18:35:10Z:
> The problem is that we are trying to introduce NDF _after_ IPPR is GA. Version N control plane is blocking admission requests where `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` FG is not present. But this is _not_ okay, because N-3 nodes do support IPPR, and we do not want control plane to block the request in all cases.

wouldn't this be a problem for any feature that went to beta, but then we discovered a blocker that needs to be restricting certain nodes from using the feature? Will the approach of two NDFs instead of one (Feature enabled, but feature is not working on this type of nodes) be preferable?
---
[c14] @natasha41575 2026-02-06T18:37:00Z:
> wouldn't this be a problem for any feature that went to beta, but then we discovered a blocker that needs to be restricting certain nodes from using the feature?

Yeah exactly, NDF is only useful for this case if we know what the restrictions need to be at the start. This is what I was trying to get across in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135329#issuecomment-3752011625
---
[c15] @pravk03 2026-02-06T18:37:31Z:
> If there is a net-new feature, I think NDF can be used for these cases. The problem is that IPPR was implemented pre-NDF.

@natasha41575 I think we would have a problem with `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature gate even if it were introduced as a declared feature after NDF was GA. The problem here is that `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` is selectively used to determine if guaranteed QOS pod can be resized. A guaranteed pod resize on an older node with static CPU policy disabled would be incorrectly blocked. 
---
[c16] @natasha41575 2026-02-06T18:39:02Z:
> > If there is a net-new feature, I think NDF can be used for these cases. The problem is that IPPR was implemented pre-NDF.
> 
> [@natasha41575](https://github.com/natasha41575) I think we would have a problem with `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature gate even if it were introduced as a declared feature after NDF was GA. The problem here is that `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` is selectively used to determine if guaranteed QOS pod can be resized. A guaranteed pod resize on an older node with static CPU policy disabled would be incorrectly blocked.

Ah I meant if NDF existed when IPPR itself was in alpha and we used it in this case all the way back then. In which case older nodes wouldn't have supported IPPR at all. But I think @SergeyKanzhelev's point is it will be impossible to always know in advance, during the development of alpha features, all the cases where we might need this.

so would the better fix be to add two variables instead of one? One saying that `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` present, another is saying `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResizeBUT_THE_NODE_IS_STATIC` - disabling the resize

> so would the better fix be to add two variables instead of one? One saying that `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` present, another is saying `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResizeBUT_THE_NODE_IS_STATIC` - disabling the resize

I'm struggling to understand how we would implement this without running into the same problem
---

> > so would the better fix be to add two variables instead of one? One saying that `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` present, another is saying `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResizeBUT_THE_NODE_IS_STATIC` - disabling the resize
>

If only `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` defined in NDF - still allow. If both defined - disallow.

> If both defined - disallow.

comments.author: tallclair
comments.body:
The `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` node declared feature isn't just tied to the `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature gate: it declares the feature if the feature gate is enabled OR the node doesn't use static CPU policy, and then requires the feature gate for all CPU resizes of guaranteed pods.

Here is the problem:
- v1.34 node: in-place pod resize is enabled, static policy disabled
	- 1.34 is pre-NDF, so it doesn't declare any features
- v1.35 control plane: NDF disabled (still alpha)
	- resizing guaranteed pod CPU is allowed (no NDF admission check), node doesn't mark resize as infeasible since it doesn't have static CPU policy.
- Upgrade cluster to v1.36: NDF goes beta & default enabled
	- Now resizing a guaranteed pod's CPU requires the `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize`, but the v1.34 node still doesn't set it, causing a regression.

I don't think we need to fix this in v1.35 since NDF is still alpha, but this is a beta-blocker.

/assign @pravk03 
/cc @natasha41575 
/milestone v1.36

comments.author: natasha41575
comments.body:
An idea I was toying around with when thinking about the other resize feasibility checks was inverting the logic: instead of the resize requiring a node declared feature to be set, the resize could be rejected if a feature is set.

In this case:
- Surface the node declared feature `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUsDisabled` (or whatever name) if the node uses static CPU policy AND the feature gate is disabled
- During admission, *reject* the resize if the node declared feature `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUsDisabled` is set

That way:
- ~with 1.36 control plane and 1.34 kubelet: the node declared feature will not be set, the patch will be permitted, and the 1.34 kubelet would run its feasibility checks (which would reject the resize as Infeasible)~
- with 1.36 control plane and 1.36 kubelet: the node declared feature *will* be set, and the patch will be rejected. 

Just my two cents!

ETA: Synced with Praveen offline, and have come to the understanding that ideally we would not rely on the kubelet checks in the old node, which makes sense.

comments.author: pravk03
comments.body: This is an issue with `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` because it depends on both feature gate and node config and NDF is not GA. If the declared feature relied solely on the feature gate (like [InPlacePodLevelResourcesVerticalScaling](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/8d450ef773127374148abad4daaf28dac6cb2625/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/nodedeclaredfeatures/features/inplacepodresize/pod_level_resource_resize.go)), this is not a problem.

comments.author: pravk03
comments.body:
> Surface the node declared feature InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs (or whatever name) if the node uses static CPU policy AND the feature gate is disabled

I think we would still run into the same issue as `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature graduates to Beta/GA.  I do not think its a good idea to have declared features based on inverse of feature gates.

comments.author: AadiDev005
comments.body:
It looks like the core challenge is the inconsistent behavior caused by the interplay of feature gates and node-declared features (NDF), especially across different Kubernetes versions.

One rough idea I’m considering is the concept of inverting the logic for the node declared feature: instead of requiring the feature to be set to allow resize, we reject the resize if an "exclusive CPUs disabled" feature is set on the node. This could help handle older nodes and avoid relying solely on kubelet checks in legacy versions.

I’d love to get feedback on this approach or any alternative ideas you think might make sense before digging deeper.

comments.author: tallclair
comments.body: @AadiDev005 was that an AI generated comment? It looks like you're just paraphrasing earlier comments and presenting the ideas as your own 😞

comments.author: tallclair
comments.body:
I think as it is, NodeDeclaredFeatures (NDF) doesn't match this use case. The problem stems from the fact that at the API level we're tightening the restrictions, by forbidding something that used to be allowed (resizing guaranteed pod CPU). This mostly stems from the fact that NDF didn't exist when we first introduced the feature gate for static CPU resize. If we had this feature gate from the beginning, it wouldn't have been an issue.

I think @natasha41575's suggestion to invert the logic, to have "Forbidden Features" rather than "Required Features" could be used for this, but I'm not sure we want to go that route. It's sort of weird for nodes to start advertising that they don't support a feature, since that implies that any node not advertising the negative feature DOES support it? Can we ever remove it in that case? Maybe this would be useful functionality to have for deprecations?

comments.author: pravk03
comments.body: Would it be acceptable to tighten the restrictions with NDF if there are existing Kubelet validations for the same feature ?. Specifically in the case of `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize`, the Kubelet currently marks resize requests with static policy as infeasible on nodes without NDF ([here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/5bcb7599736327cd8c6d23e398002354a6e40f68/pkg/kubelet/allocation/allocation_manager.go#L693)), whereas on nodes with NDF, we reject the request during admission. While this admission behavior is inconsistent, it should resolve once NDF is enabled on all nodes. From the Pod's perspective, the net effect with and without NDF is the same ?

comments.author: tallclair
comments.body: Yeah, I think that's OK. In that case, we're just shifting the error to surface earlier. The problem we encountered in this issue is that pods that _wouldn't_ be marked infeasible can be rejected.

comments.author: natasha41575
comments.body:
> This mostly stems from the fact that NDF didn't exist when we first introduced the feature gate for static CPU resize.

I wonder if we should just state that NDF can't be used retroactively to block admission requests that would have previously succeeded. Net-new features (like PLR + IPPR) can make use of NDF if they are baked into the initial implementation/design, but otherwise it doesn't seem to fit the use case. 

This would make NDF useless for moving IPPR feasibility checks ... originally I was hoping it could be useful for `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize`, an analogous `GuaranteedQoSPodMemoryResize`, and maybe even resize + swap. But maybe not...

comments.author: pravk03
comments.body:
(Capturing discussions from slack and meetings)

The main concern here is that admission selectively depends on a feature gate, and NDF does not work well in such cases. 

Currently, `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` is declared by the node when the below conditions are met 
- `InPlacePodVerticalScalingExclusiveCPUs` feature gate is enabled and Atatic CPU policy is enabled
**OR**
- Static CPU policy is disabled (feature gate is irrelevant here).

Since new declared features are not added on older nodes, requests that were previously allowed - specifically when the feature gate is irrelevant, would start to fail after the declared feature is added.

Based on the discussions, its better to stop declaring features that selectively depend on feature gates. I will make a change to stop declaring [GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1861c1a07244e8e9430aaf588722dd22287c471e/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/nodedeclaredfeatures/features/inplacepodresize/guaranteed_cpu_resize.go)

comments.body:

what kind of feedback does this gives us? What would be the "correct" way of using NDF in cases like this going forward?

comments.author: natasha41575
comments.body:
> > Based on the discussions, its better to stop declaring features that selectively depend on feature gates. I will make a change to stop declaring [GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/1861c1a07244e8e9430aaf588722dd22287c471e/staging/src/k8s.io/component-helpers/nodedeclaredfeatures/features/inplacepodresize/guaranteed_cpu_resize.go)
> 
> what kind of feedback does this gives us? What would be the "correct" way of using NDF in cases like this going forward?

If there is a net-new feature, I think NDF can be used for these cases. The problem is that IPPR was implemented pre-NDF.

Say we had NDF at the time that IPPR was being implemented and we had used it. Version N control plane would selectively block admission requests where `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` FG was not present. This is okay, because N-3 nodes would not have permitted IPPR at all, because it was not a supported feature. 

The problem is that we are trying to introduce NDF _after_ IPPR is GA. Version N control plane is blocking admission requests where `GuaranteedQoSPodCPUResize` FG is not present. But this is _not_ okay, because N-3 nodes do support IPPR, and we do not want control plane to block the request in all cases. 

For these cases, I think it just means that we have to wait for NDF to be GA+3.

comments.body:

wouldn't this be a problem for any feature that went to beta, but then we discovered a blocker that needs to be restricting certain nodes from using the feature? Will the approach of two NDFs instead of one (Feature enabled, but feature is not working on this type of nodes) be preferable?

Yeah exactly, NDF is only useful for this case if we know what the restrictions need to be at the start. This is what I was trying to get across in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/135329#issuecomment-3752011625

title: [Failing Test] [sig-node] Container Runtime Conformance Test container runtime conformance blackbox test when running a container with a new image should be able to pull from private registry with credential provider
need_summary: Whether the private-registry credential-provider conformance test was failing because of stale kubelet credential caching and a too-short timeout, anchored on the proposed fixes in GitHub PR #135125 and PR #135142 plus the related test logs.
security_topic: credential cache race causing private registry image pull failure
question_text: After replacing localhost with 127.0.0.1, the network connectivity is resolved. but the kubelet is still failing to pull the image from the registry.
answer_text: 1. Kubelet's credential provider caches docker credentials for 5 minutes 2. Test writes config.json after kubelet has already cached empty credentials 3. First image pull uses stale cache (no credentials) → fails with auth error 4. Cache refreshes after 5 minutes and finds the credentials, By then, pod is already in ImagePullBackOff state 5. node.ContainerStatusRetryTimeout is 5m, the test will fail because of the race condition between credential cache refresh and the test timeout. I created a [draft PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135125) to increase the timeout to 10m. Waiting for the test results. pull-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd is green: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/135125/pull-kubernetes-node-e2e-containerd/1986018307521646592 but pull-kubernetes-node-crio-e2e is red. https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/135125/pull-kubernetes-node-crio-e2e/1986018307597144064

title: ServiceAccount with RoleBinding only can delete its namespace
need_summary: Whether a namespace-scoped RoleBinding can let a ServiceAccount delete its own namespace, and the answer is that Kubernetes RBAC is designed to allow Roles to write within their namespace with a suggested ValidatingAdmissionPolicy workaround.
security_topic: RBAC behavior for namespace deletion with namespace-scoped bindings
question_text: I have a question. What would be the behavior if we bind a cluster role to a namespace scoped role binding. Will the delete namespace access be restricted or allowed.
answer_text:
Although it can be really surprising, RBAC in Kubernetes is designed – I think – to allow Roles to be able to write to their namespace.

If you don't want this, you can use a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy that restricts it.

There isn't a feature where you can configure the granting-admin-allows-namespace-writes behavior.

---

If we did a Kubernetes 2.0, making authz more flexible would be a nice improvement. Kubernetes' implementation of RBAC just has too many gotchas to leave it unchanged.

Although it can be really surprising, RBAC in Kubernetes is designed – I think – to allow Roles to be able to write to their namespace.

If you don't want this, you can use a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy that restricts it.

There isn't a feature where you can configure the granting-admin-allows-namespace-writes behavior.

---

If we did a Kubernetes 2.0, making authz more flexible would be a nice improvement. Kubernetes' implementation of RBAC just has too many gotchas to leave it unchanged.

title: Kube-proxy(IPVS) v1.31.0 fails to add KUBE-LOOP-BACK ipset entry for hairpin traffic, causing SNAT failure
need_summary: Whether the hairpin SNAT failure was actually caused by a missing KUBE-LOOP-BACK client-server entry or by the required bridge-nf-call-iptables sysctl, as explained in the maintainer’s answer in comments c5 and c7.
security_topic: expected behavior of kube-proxy hairpin SNAT handling
question_text:
Hi @danwinship, thanks very much! 

`sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1` immediately fixed the issue.

I just have one follow-up question regarding my original analysis: Is the current behavior of `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` (only containing server-pod-ip,port,server-pod-ip) actually the expected design?

I originally suspected it was a bug because the set didn't contain an entry for the client pod (server-ip,port,client-ip). Does enabling the sysctl mean that kube-proxy is not required to maintain specific client-server pair entries in the ipset to handle this traffic correctly?
answer_text:
Yes, `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` is only supposed to have entries for self-to-self.

The issue in both cases is that if a packet gets DNATted on the outbound path, we have to make sure that its reply path takes it somewhere where it will get un-DNATted before it gets back to the client pod.

kube-proxy breaks that into two cases:
- If the client pod and the server pod are _the same pod_, then if kube-proxy were to DNAT the pod and not masquerade it, then it would end up getting sent back to the pod with the source and destination IP both set to the pod's IP, so when the pod replied, it would try to send the reply directly to itself, and then fail. So to prevent that from happening, kube-proxy masquerades the packet as well, so now when the pod receives it, it thinks the packet came from the node IP, not from itself, so it sends the reply back out to the node, and then it gets un-DNATted and un-masqueraded and then routed back to the pod. This is what `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` is for.
- If the client pod and the server pod are _different pods_, then kube-proxy assumes that the reply from the server to the client will come back out to the host network namespace, and the DNAT will get undone there, so everything will just work. But if the client and server are on a bridge, and that bridge _doesn't_ have `bridge-nf-call-iptables` set, then the reply packet will just immediately go from the server to the client without letting iptables/conntrack un-DNAT it first, causing your problem. Setting `bridge-nf-call-iptables` fixes it, by making the bridge properly un-DNAT the reply packet before passing it on to the client.

Hacking `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` the way you did works around the problem by just causing _all_ local packets to get masqueraded, so then even in the "different pods" case, the reply packet has to get sent all way back off the bridge to the host network namespace. But it's inefficient because (a) you're making the return packet path longer, and (b) you're making the `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` set bigger.

ISSUE #134884: Kube-proxy(IPVS) v1.31.0 fails to add KUBE-LOOP-BACK ipset entry for hairpin traffic, causing SNAT failure Author: czczcz831 Date: 2025-10-25T16:48:05Z Labels: kind/bug, sig/network, needs-triage State: closed [c0] ### What happened? **Kubernetes version** : `registry.k8s.io/kube-proxy:v1.31.0` We are running a minimal two-node cluster set up with `kubeadm`: one control-plane node (Ubuntu) and one worker node (Debian). When a Pod tries to connect to a Service (ClusterIP), the connection behavior depends entirely on the client's location: - **Cross-node access (Works):** Connections from the control-plane node to the Service IP (`10.104.26.46`) succeed. - **Same-node access (Fails):** When a client Pod (`10.244.0.103`) tries to connect to the Service IP, and the backing Pod (`10.244.0.71`) is scheduled on the _same worker node_, the connection fails. The cluster is running `kube-proxy` in **`ipvs` mode**. **Evidence:** 1. **`tcpdump`** on the node shows the client Pod (`10.244.0.103`) sends a `[SYN]` to the Service IP (`10.104.26.46`). This packet is correctly DNATed to the server Pod IP (`10.244.0.71`). 2. The server Pod (`.71`) replies with a `[SYN, ACK]` directly to the client Pod (`.103`). 3. The client Pod (`.103`) immediately sends a `[RST]` because it received a reply from an unexpected IP (`.71`) instead of the Service IP (`.46`) it initiated the connection with. _This confirms a **SNAT failure** for the hairpin traffic._ 4. In `ipvs` mode, `kube-proxy` still relies on `iptables` and `ipset` for hairpin SNAT. The `iptables` rules in `KUBE-POSTROUTING` correctly point to an `ipset` named `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` to handle this: ```bash root@CZDebian1:~# iptables-save -t nat ... -A KUBE-POSTROUTING -m comment --comment "Kubernetes endpoints dst ip:port, source ip for solving hairpin purpose" -m set --match-set KUBE-LOOP-BACK dst,dst,src -j MASQUERADE ... ``` 5. However, checking the `ipset` reveals that `kube-proxy` **fails to add the required entry** for the client/server Pod pair: ```bash # ipset list KUBE-LOOP-BACK | grep 10.244.0.71 10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.71 # The required (dst-ip, dst-port, src-ip) rule is missing, # expected missing entry: 10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.103 ``` Crucially, when manually adding the correct entry for debugging, the connection is temporarily fixed. ```bash # ipset add KUBE-LOOP-BACK 10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.110 # At this point, the connection from ...110 works ``` However, within seconds, kube-proxy's reconciliation loop runs, compares the state to its (incorrect) "expected state", and actively deletes the manually added entry, calling it "legacy". This proves its internal logic is flawed. ```bash # kube-proxy logs show: I1025 14:07:28.276446 1 ipset.go:174] "Successfully deleted legacy ip set entry from ip set" ipSetEntry="10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.103" ipSet="KUBE-LOOP-BACK" I1025 14:08:26.203177 1 ipset.go:174] "Successfully deleted legacy ip set entry from ip set" ipSetEntry="10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.110" ipSet="KUBE-LOOP-BACK" ``` ### What did you expect to happen? `kube-proxy` should correctly identify that the client Pod (`.103` / `.110`) and the server Pod (`.71`) are on the same node. It should then **create and persist** the required SNAT rule in the `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` `ipset` (e.g., `10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.110`). It should _not_ delete manually added, correct entries, as this indicates a flaw in its reconciliation logic. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. Set up a minimal Kubernetes cluster (e.g., v1.31.0) using `kubeadm` with one control-plane node and one worker node. 2. Configure `kube-proxy` to run in `ipvs` mode (e.g., by patching the `kube-proxy` ConfigMap or during `kubeadm init` via the `KubeProxyConfiguration`). 3. Ensure the `kube-proxy` configuration uses the default `iptables.masqueradeAll: false`. 4. Deploy a server application (e.g., `nginx` or `mysql`) and expose it via a ClusterIP Service. 5. Using a `nodeSelector` or `nodeName`, ensure this server pod (**`Pod-Server`**) is scheduled and running on the **worker node**. 6. Deploy two client/debug pods using an image that includes `netcat`, such as `nicolaka/netshoot:latest`: * Schedule one pod (**`Pod-Client-A`**) onto the **worker node** (the same node as `Pod-Server`). * Schedule the other pod (**`Pod-Client-B`**) onto the **control-plane node**. 7. **Test cross-node connection (baseline):** * Exec into `Pod-Client-B` (on the control-plane) and connect to the server's ClusterIP: ```bash kubectl exec -it -- nc -zv ``` * **Result:** The connection **SUCCEEDS**, as expected. 8. **Test same-node (hairpin) connection (the bug):** * Exec into `Pod-Client-A` (on the worker node) and connect to the *same* ClusterIP: ```bash kubectl exec -it -- nc -zv ``` * **Actual Result:** The connection **FAILS** (e.g., times out). 9. **Investigate on the worker node:** * SSH into the **worker node** (where `Pod-Server` and `Pod-Client-A` are running). * Run `ipset list KUBE-LOOP-BACK`. * **Observation:** The set is missing the required entry for this connection. An entry for `,tcp:,` does not exist (though an entry for pod-to-self, `,tcp:,`, may exist). 10. **Apply manual fix:** * On the **worker node**, manually add the missing `ipset` entry: ```bash ipset add KUBE-LOOP-BACK ,tcp:, ``` 11. **Verify manual fix:** * Immediately re-run the test from `Pod-Client-A`: ```bash kubectl exec -it -- nc -zv ``` * **Result:** The connection **SUCCEEDS** immediately. 12. **Confirm `kube-proxy` rollback:** * Wait for the `kube-proxy` sync interval (e.g., \~30-60 seconds). * Check the `kube-proxy` pod logs on the worker node, observing messages about ipset changes (e.g., "Successfully deleted legacy ip set entry"). * Run `ipset list KUBE-LOOP-BACK` again on the worker node. * **Result:** The manually added entry has been removed by `kube-proxy`, and the connection from `Pod-Client-A` will begin failing again. ### Anything else we need to know? This appears to be a bug in `kube-proxy`'s logic, as all related configurations have been verified as correct: - **`kubelet` Config:** `hairpinMode: "hairpin-veth"` - **`kube-proxy` Pod Args:** `command: --hostname-override=$(NODE_NAME)` and `env: NODE_NAME: (v1:spec.nodeName)` - **`kube-proxy` ConfigMap:** `mode: "ipvs"`, `clusterCIDR: "10.244.0.0/16"` - **`Node` Object:** `PodCIDR: 10.244.0.0/24` (and both Pods are in this CIDR) - **Client `Pod` Object:** `spec.nodeName` correctly matches the node name (`czdebian1`) - **`Service` Object:** `internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` **Workaround:** The only workaround found was to edit the `kube-proxy` ConfigMap and set **`iptables.masqueradeAll: true`**. This bypasses the broken `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` logic by SNAT-ing _all_ Pod traffic, which incidentally covers the hairpin case. This confirms the bug is specific to the `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` ipset population logic when `masqueradeAll` is false. ### Kubernetes version

comments.author: czczcz831
comments.body:
### What happened? **Kubernetes version** : `registry.k8s.io/kube-proxy:v1.31.0` We are running a minimal two-node cluster set up with `kubeadm`: one control-plane node (Ubuntu) and one worker node (Debian). When a Pod tries to connect to a Service (ClusterIP), the connection behavior depends entirely on the client's location: - **Cross-node access (Works):** Connections from the control-plane node to the Service IP (`10.104.26.46`) succeed. - **Same-node access (Fails):** When a client Pod (`10.244.0.103`) tries to connect to the Service IP, and the backing Pod (`10.244.0.71`) is scheduled on the _same worker node_, the connection fails. The cluster is running `kube-proxy` in **`ipvs` mode**. **Evidence:** 1. **`tcpdump`** on the node shows the client Pod (`10.244.0.103`) sends a `[SYN]` to the Service IP (`10.104.26.46`). This packet is correctly DNATed to the server Pod IP (`10.244.0.71`). 2. The server Pod (`.71`) replies with a `[SYN, ACK]` directly to the client Pod (`.103`). 3. The client Pod (`.103`) immediately sends a `[RST]` because it received a reply from an unexpected IP (`.71`) instead of the Service IP (`.46`) it initiated the connection with. _This confirms a **SNAT failure** for the hairpin traffic._ 4. In `ipvs` mode, `kube-proxy` still relies on `iptables` and `ipset` for hairpin SNAT. The `iptables` rules in `KUBE-POSTROUTING` correctly point to an `ipset` named `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` to handle this: ```bash root@CZDebian1:~# iptables-save -t nat ... -A KUBE-POSTROUTING -m comment --comment "Kubernetes endpoints dst ip:port, source ip for solving hairpin purpose" -m set --match-set KUBE-LOOP-BACK dst,dst,src -j MASQUERADE ... ``` 5. However, checking the `ipset` reveals that `kube-proxy` **fails to add the required entry** for the client/server Pod pair: ```bash # ipset list KUBE-LOOP-BACK | grep 10.244.0.71 10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.71 # The required (dst-ip, dst-port, src-ip) rule is missing, # expected missing entry: 10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.103 ``` Crucially, when manually adding the correct entry for debugging, the connection is temporarily fixed. ```bash # ipset add KUBE-LOOP-BACK 10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.110 # At this point, the connection from ...110 works ``` However, within seconds, kube-proxy's reconciliation loop runs, compares the state to its (incorrect) "expected state", and actively deletes the manually added entry, calling it "legacy". This proves its internal logic is flawed. ```bash # kube-proxy logs show: I1025 14:07:28.276446 1 ipset.go:174] "Successfully deleted legacy ip set entry from ip set" ipSetEntry="10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.103" ipSet="KUBE-LOOP-BACK" I1025 14:08:26.203177 1 ipset.go:174] "Successfully deleted legacy ip set entry from ip set" ipSetEntry="10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.110" ipSet="KUBE-LOOP-BACK" ``` ### What did you expect to happen? `kube-proxy` should correctly identify that the client Pod (`.103` / `.110`) and the server Pod (`.71`) are on the same node. It should then **create and persist** the required SNAT rule in the `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` `ipset` (e.g., `10.244.0.71,tcp:3306,10.244.0.110`). It should _not_ delete manually added, correct entries, as this indicates a flaw in its reconciliation logic. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? 1. Set up a minimal Kubernetes cluster (e.g., v1.31.0) using `kubeadm` with one control-plane node and one worker node. 2. Configure `kube-proxy` to run in `ipvs` mode (e.g., by patching the `kube-proxy` ConfigMap or during `kubeadm init` via the `KubeProxyConfiguration`). 3. Ensure the `kube-proxy` configuration uses the default `iptables.masqueradeAll: false`. 4. Deploy a server application (e.g., `nginx` or `mysql`) and expose it via a ClusterIP Service. 5. Using a `nodeSelector` or `nodeName`, ensure this server pod (**`Pod-Server`**) is scheduled and running on the **worker node**. 6. Deploy two client/debug pods using an image that includes `netcat`, such as `nicolaka/netshoot:latest`: * Schedule one pod (**`Pod-Client-A`**) onto the **worker node** (the same node as `Pod-Server`). * Schedule the other pod (**`Pod-Client-B`**) onto the **control-plane node**. 7. **Test cross-node connection (baseline):** * Exec into `Pod-Client-B` (on the control-plane) and connect to the server's ClusterIP: ```bash kubectl exec -it -- nc -zv ``` * **Result:** The connection **SUCCEEDS**, as expected. 8. **Test same-node (hairpin) connection (the bug):** * Exec into `Pod-Client-A` (on the worker node) and connect to the *same* ClusterIP: ```bash kubectl exec -it -- nc -zv ``` * **Actual Result:** The connection **FAILS** (e.g., times out). 9. **Investigate on the worker node:** * SSH into the **worker node** (where `Pod-Server` and `Pod-Client-A` are running). * Run `ipset list KUBE-LOOP-BACK`. * **Observation:** The set is missing the required entry for this connection. An entry for `,tcp:,` does not exist (though an entry for pod-to-self, `,tcp:,`, may exist). 10. **Apply manual fix:** * On the **worker node**, manually add the missing `ipset` entry: ```bash ipset add KUBE-LOOP-BACK ,tcp:, ``` 11. **Verify manual fix:** * Immediately re-run the test from `Pod-Client-A`: ```bash kubectl exec -it -- nc -zv ``` * **Result:** The connection **SUCCEEDS** immediately. 12. **Confirm `kube-proxy` rollback:** * Wait for the `kube-proxy` sync interval (e.g., \~30-60 seconds). * Check the `kube-proxy` pod logs on the worker node, observing messages about ipset changes (e.g., "Successfully deleted legacy ip set entry"). * Run `ipset list KUBE-LOOP-BACK` again on the worker node. * **Result:** The manually added entry has been removed by `kube-proxy`, and the connection from `Pod-Client-A` will begin failing again. ### Anything else we need to know? This appears to be a bug in `kube-proxy`'s logic, as all related configurations have been verified as correct: - **`kubelet` Config:** `hairpinMode: "hairpin-veth"` - **`kube-proxy` Pod Args:** `command: --hostname-override=$(NODE_NAME)` and `env: NODE_NAME: (v1:spec.nodeName)` - **`kube-proxy` ConfigMap:** `mode: "ipvs"`, `clusterCIDR: "10.244.0.0/16"` - **`Node` Object:** `PodCIDR: 10.244.0.0/24` (and both Pods are in this CIDR) - **Client `Pod` Object:** `spec.nodeName` correctly matches the node name (`czdebian1`) - **`Service` Object:** `internalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` **Workaround:** The only workaround found was to edit the `kube-proxy` ConfigMap and set **`iptables.masqueradeAll: true`**. This bypasses the broken `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` logic by SNAT-ing _all_ Pod traffic, which incidentally covers the hairpin case. This confirms the bug is specific to the `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` ipset population logic when `masqueradeAll` is false. ### Kubernetes version
```console root@CZHomeServer:~# kubectl version Client Version: v1.31.0 Kustomize Version: v5.4.2 Server Version: v1.31.0 ```
### Cloud provider
Build a kubeadm cluster locally, one worker node and one control plane node
### OS version
```console # On Linux: $ cat /etc/os-release root@CZHomeServer:~# cat /etc/os-release PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS" NAME="Ubuntu" VERSION_ID="22.04" VERSION="22.04.4 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish)" VERSION_CODENAME=jammy ID=ubuntu ID_LIKE=debian HOME_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/" SUPPORT_URL="https://help.ubuntu.com/" BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/" PRIVACY_POLICY_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/legal/terms-and-policies/privacy-policy" UBUNTU_CODENAME=jammyu $ uname -a root@CZHomeServer:~# uname -a Linux CZHomeServer 6.8.0-85-generic #85~22.04.1-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Fri Sep 19 16:18:59 UTC 2 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux root@CZDebian1:~# cat /etc/os-release PRETTY_NAME="Debian GNU/Linux 12 (bookworm)" NAME="Debian GNU/Linux" VERSION_ID="12" VERSION="12 (bookworm)" VERSION_CODENAME=bookworm ID=debian HOME_URL="https://www.debian.org/" SUPPORT_URL="https://www.debian.org/support" BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.debian.org/" root@CZDebian1:~# uname -a Linux CZDebian1 6.1.0-37-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Debian 6.1.140-1 (2025-05-22) x86_64 GNU/Linux ```

kube-proxy ```bash root@CZHomeServer:~# kubectl get daemonset kube-proxy -n kube-system -o yaml | grep 'image:' image: registry.k8s.io/kube-proxy:v1.31.0 ``` kubectl ```bash root@CZHomeServer:~# kubectl version --client --output=yaml clientVersion: buildDate: "2024-08-13T07:37:34Z" compiler: gc gitCommit: 9edcffcde5595e8a5b1a35f88c421764e575afce gitTreeState: clean gitVersion: v1.31.0 goVersion: go1.22.5 major: "1" minor: "31" platform: linux/amd64 kustomizeVersion: v5.4.2 ``` kubeadm ```bash kubeadm version: &version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"31", GitVersion:"v1.31.0", GitCommit:"9edcffcde5595e8a5b1a35f88c421764e575afce", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2024-08-13T07:35:57Z", GoVersion:"go1.22.5", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} ```

comments.author: Adarsh1337
comments.body:
This is an excellent bug report with comprehensive analysis. I've encountered similar IPVS hairpin traffic issues in production environments. Based on the detailed investigation, this appears to be a logic flaw in the kube-proxy's IPVS reconciliation loop when determining which client-server Pod pairs require KUBE-LOOP-BACK ipset entries.

## Technical Analysis

The root cause is in kube-proxy's `proxier.syncIPSetEntries()` method where it builds the expected state for the KUBE-LOOP-BACK ipset. The logic incorrectly evaluates same-node Pod-to-Service traffic patterns, specifically:

1. **Missing Entry Generation**: The algorithm fails to recognize when a client Pod and server Pod are co-located on the same node and need hairpin SNAT
2. **Incorrect State Reconciliation**: The "legacy entry" deletion confirms the reconciler believes the manually-added correct entry shouldn't exist
3. **Node Locality Detection**: The issue likely stems from improper node name/IP correlation during endpoint enumeration

## Proposed Solutions

### Immediate Fix
The bug is likely in `pkg/proxy/ipvs/proxier.go` in the `syncIPSetEntries` function. The logic for determining same-node relationships between client and server endpoints needs investigation around:

```go
// Pseudo-code location of likely bug
for _, ep := range endpoints {
    if shouldAddLoopBackEntry(clientNodeName, ep.NodeName) {
        // This condition is likely failing
    }
}
```

### Code Areas to Investigate
1. **proxier.go:syncIPSetEntries()** - Primary suspect for missing entry generation
2. **endpointsInfo node tracking** - Verify proper node name propagation from kubelet
3. **IPVS service topology awareness** - Ensure same-node detection logic is sound

### Testing Strategy
I recommend adding unit tests specifically for:
- Same-node client/server endpoint scenarios
- KUBE-LOOP-BACK ipset entry generation logic
- Edge cases with multiple Pods per node

This impacts production clusters significantly as hairpin traffic is common in microservices architectures. The workaround of `masqueradeAll: true` works but introduces unnecessary SNAT overhead for all traffic.

**Priority**: High - affects core networking functionality in IPVS mode
**Impact**: Service mesh, multi-tenant clusters, and dense Pod deployments

I'd be happy to investigate the exact code paths and provide a patch if maintainers can confirm this analysis aligns with the expected behavior.

comments.author: danwinship
comments.body:
You need to do `sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1`.

kubeadm used to do this itself, but that was wrong because most plugins don't need it (and don't want it; it slightly reduces network throughput), and besides, the network plugins that _do_ need it ought to set it themselves rather than expect the user's cluster-deployment tool to have done it.

Flannel apparently currently documents the fact that you need to load the `br-netfilter` kernel module (which is true), and checks for that at startup (by seeing if the `net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables` sysctl exists), but it _doesn't_ document the fact that that sysctl needs to be set to `1`.

I'm going to add a comment to https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel/issues/2068.

comments.author: czczcz831
comments.body:
Hi @danwinship, thanks very much! 

`sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables=1` immediately fixed the issue.

I just have one follow-up question regarding my original analysis: Is the current behavior of `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` (only containing server-pod-ip,port,server-pod-ip) actually the expected design?

I originally suspected it was a bug because the set didn't contain an entry for the client pod (server-ip,port,client-ip). Does enabling the sysctl mean that kube-proxy is not required to maintain specific client-server pair entries in the ipset to handle this traffic correctly?

comments.author: danwinship
comments.body:
Yes, `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` is only supposed to have entries for self-to-self.

The issue in both cases is that if a packet gets DNATted on the outbound path, we have to make sure that its reply path takes it somewhere where it will get un-DNATted before it gets back to the client pod.

kube-proxy breaks that into two cases:
- If the client pod and the server pod are _the same pod_, then if kube-proxy were to DNAT the pod and not masquerade it, then it would end up getting sent back to the pod with the source and destination IP both set to the pod's IP, so when the pod replied, it would try to send the reply directly to itself, and then fail. So to prevent that from happening, kube-proxy masquerades the packet as well, so now when the pod receives it, it thinks the packet came from the node IP, not from itself, so it sends the reply back out to the node, and then it gets un-DNATted and un-masqueraded and then routed back to the pod. This is what `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` is for.
- If the client pod and the server pod are _different pods_, then kube-proxy assumes that the reply from the server to the client will come back out to the host network namespace, and the DNAT will get undone there, so everything will just work. But if the client and server are on a bridge, and that bridge _doesn't_ have `bridge-nf-call-iptables` set, then the reply packet will just immediately go from the server to the client without letting iptables/conntrack un-DNAT it first, causing your problem. Setting `bridge-nf-call-iptables` fixes it, by making the bridge properly un-DNAT the reply packet before passing it on to the client.

Hacking `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` the way you did works around the problem by just causing _all_ local packets to get masqueraded, so then even in the "different pods" case, the reply packet has to get sent all way back off the bridge to the host network namespace. But it's inefficient because (a) you're making the return packet path longer, and (b) you're making the `KUBE-LOOP-BACK` set bigger.

title: (DRA) Requests field not set for config FromClass in ResourceClaim.status.allocation.devices.config
need_summary: Whether the ResourceClaim device config bug that could mislead DRA drivers is fixed across supported Kubernetes branches, with the concrete anchors being the backport PRs #135098, #135105, and #135109.
security_topic: device config attribution bug causing potential misrouting in DRA drivers
question_text: When creating a ResourceClaim with 2 requests with 2 different device class that have a config, the config reported in the allocation devices status is not mentioning from which request the config is coming from. So the DRA-Drivers cannot identify the configuration belonging to the request it is supposed to handle.
answer_text: This is broken also in older Kubernetes releases. It can potentially cause misbehavior in DRA drivers (they treat the config as applying to all requests) with unknown consequences, so this should get backported to all supported release branches.
thread_text:
ISSUE #134789: (DRA) Requests field not set for config FromClass in ResourceClaim.status.allocation.devices.config
Author: LionelJouin
Date: 2025-10-22T19:02:39Z
Labels: kind/bug, priority/important-soon, triage/accepted, wg/device-management
State: closed

[c0]
### What happened?

When creating a ResourceClaim with 2 requests with 2 different device class that have a config, the config reported in the allocation devices status is not mentioning from which request the config is coming from. question_text:
I'm trying to create a [simple](https://github.com/everzakov/dra-plugin-health-example/tree/main) DRA plugin with ReasourceHealthStatus feature. However, kubelet do not report health status for resource claim generated by resource claim template (also if resource claim object has another name then resource name in pod spec).

If i understand correctly, the problem is related to this resource claim name [comparison](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/dra/manager.go#L811). In container.Resources.Claims claim.Name is pod spec defined when claimInfo.ClaimName is a Object [Name](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/resourceclaim/resourceclaim.go#L65).
answer_text: This behavior you have found is indeed a bug. You can try replacing the logic in dra/manager.go with [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134875) new logic soon which should get the proper claim names. I am also adding more e2e testing that will specifically safeguard for this now.  The PR is a WIP for now, will cc you and update once ready.

title: apiserver: stats.go Error getting keys. Too large resource version
need_summary: Whether the apiserver errors are caused by a known watch-cache/consistent-read issue in Kubernetes and etcd v3.5.6, anchored by the maintainer’s explanation and the linked Kubernetes blog post about consistent read from cache requiring etcd v3.5.13+.
security_topic: consistent-read cache errors tied to etcd version compatibility
question_text:
In a clean install of a k8s 1.34.1 we get this error a lot:
```
answer_text:
This is the reason for the issue in your cluster. You are running 3 year old etcd version that has a bug preventing consistent reads from cache from working. You need at least etcd v3.5.13 for consistent reads to work.

https://kubernetes.io/blog/2024/08/15/consistent-read-from-cache-beta/

title: Unable to set PriorityClass via MutatingAdmissionPolicy
need_summary: Whether the MutatingAdmissionPolicy/Priority admission interaction is a real bug and the concrete workaround is to remove `spec.priority`, as anchored by the linked Kubernetes source lines in `plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go`.
security_topic: MutatingAdmissionPolicy interaction with Priority admission defaulting
question_text:
I want to add a default priority class to workloads based on the labels of a namespace. I created the necessary resources and then tried to run a pod. I then get the following error:

Error from server (Forbidden): error when creating "/tmp/x": pods "x" is forbidden: the integer value of priority (0) must not be provided in pod spec; priority admission controller computed 1000 from the given PriorityClass name

I'm not explicitly setting priority though. See the attached resources.
answer_text:
The issue arises from the interaction between the **Priority** admission plugin's defaulting logic and the admission re-invocation loop when a `MutatingAdmissionPolicy` modifies the `priorityClassName`.

#### 1. First Admission Pass (Priority Plugin)
When the Pod is first submitted (without a `priorityClassName`), the `Priority` plugin runs. It resolves the default priority (typically `0`) and **sets the `spec.priority` field**.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L162-L171

```go
		if len(pod.Spec.PriorityClassName) == 0 {
			var err error
			var pcName string
			pcName, priority, preemptionPolicy, err = p.getDefaultPriority()
            // ...
			pod.Spec.PriorityClassName = pcName
		}
        // ...
        // [!] Sets priority to 0
		pod.Spec.Priority = &priority
```

#### 2. Mutation (MutatingAdmissionPolicy)
The `MutatingAdmissionPolicy` executes and updates `spec.priorityClassName` to the desired class (e.g., "high-priority", value `1000`). Crucially, the policy **does not unset** the `spec.priority` field; it remains `0` (from Step 1).

#### 3. Second Admission Pass (Re-invocation)
The `Priority` plugin runs again on the mutated object.
*   It observes the new `priorityClassName` ("high-priority") and resolves the correct priority value (`1000`).
*   It checks `spec.priority`. Finding it set to `0`, it compares `0` against `1000`.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L185-L187

```go
		// if the pod contained a priority that differs from the one computed from the priority class, error
		if pod.Spec.Priority != nil && *pod.Spec.Priority != priority {
			return admission.NewForbidden(a, fmt.Errorf("the integer value of priority (%d) must not be provided in pod spec; priority admission controller computed %d from the given PriorityClass name", *pod.Spec.Priority, priority))
		}
```

The plugin incorrectly assumes the mismatching `priority` (0) was explicitly provided by the user, resulting in the `Forbidden` error.

### Manual Workaround (Verified)

To work around this issue, you can modify your `MutatingAdmissionPolicy` to explicitly **remove** the `spec.priority` field when setting the `priorityClassName`. This forces the Priority plugin to re-calculate the correct priority based on the new class name.

You can achieve this by adding a `JSONPatch` mutation alongside your `applyConfiguration`.

Example `MutatingAdmissionPolicy`:

```yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: MutatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: set-priority-class
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups:   [""]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations:  ["CREATE"]
      resources:   ["pods"]
  mutations:
    # 1. Set the desired PriorityClassName
    - applyConfiguration:
        expression: "Object{spec: Object.spec{priorityClassName: 'high-priority'}}"
    
    # 2. Explicitly remove the 'priority' field to trigger re-calculation
    - jsonPatch:
        expression: '[JSONPatch{op: "remove", path: "/spec/priority"}]'
```

comments.author: lalitc375
comments.body:
### Root Cause Analysis

The issue arises from the interaction between the **Priority** admission plugin's defaulting logic and the admission re-invocation loop when a `MutatingAdmissionPolicy` modifies the `priorityClassName`.

#### 1. First Admission Pass (Priority Plugin)
When the Pod is first submitted (without a `priorityClassName`), the `Priority` plugin runs. It resolves the default priority (typically `0`) and **sets the `spec.priority` field**.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L162-L171

```go
		if len(pod.Spec.PriorityClassName) == 0 {
			var err error
			var pcName string
			pcName, priority, preemptionPolicy, err = p.getDefaultPriority()
            // ...
			pod.Spec.PriorityClassName = pcName
		}
        // ...
        // [!] Sets priority to 0
		pod.Spec.Priority = &priority
```

#### 2. Mutation (MutatingAdmissionPolicy)
The `MutatingAdmissionPolicy` executes and updates `spec.priorityClassName` to the desired class (e.g., "high-priority", value `1000`). Crucially, the policy **does not unset** the `spec.priority` field; it remains `0` (from Step 1).

#### 3. Second Admission Pass (Re-invocation)
The `Priority` plugin runs again on the mutated object.
*   It observes the new `priorityClassName` ("high-priority") and resolves the correct priority value (`1000`).
*   It checks `spec.priority`. Finding it set to `0`, it compares `0` against `1000`.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/plugin/pkg/admission/priority/admission.go#L185-L187

```go
		// if the pod contained a priority that differs from the one computed from the priority class, error
		if pod.Spec.Priority != nil && *pod.Spec.Priority != priority {
			return admission.NewForbidden(a, fmt.Errorf("the integer value of priority (%d) must not be provided in pod spec; priority admission controller computed %d from the given PriorityClass name", *pod.Spec.Priority, priority))
		}
```

The plugin incorrectly assumes the mismatching `priority` (0) was explicitly provided by the user, resulting in the `Forbidden` error.

### Manual Workaround (Verified)

To work around this issue, you can modify your `MutatingAdmissionPolicy` to explicitly **remove** the `spec.priority` field when setting the `priorityClassName`. This forces the Priority plugin to re-calculate the correct priority based on the new class name.

You can achieve this by adding a `JSONPatch` mutation alongside your `applyConfiguration`.

Example `MutatingAdmissionPolicy`:

```yaml
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: MutatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: set-priority-class
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups:   [""]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations:  ["CREATE"]
      resources:   ["pods"]
  mutations:
    # 1. Set the desired PriorityClassName
    - applyConfiguration:
        expression: "Object{spec: Object.spec{priorityClassName: 'high-priority'}}"
    
    # 2. Explicitly remove the 'priority' field to trigger re-calculation
    - jsonPatch:
        expression: '[JSONPatch{op: "remove", path: "/spec/priority"}]'
```

comments.author: ngopalak-redhat
comments.body:
The test passes (locally) after implementing two modifications:

- Changed the resources/limits/memory to 250MB.

- Enabled the MemoryQoS feature gate.

This configuration designates the Pod as Burstable, causing Kubernetes to automatically set the Cgroups `memory.high` soft limit to 90% of the 250MB limit (approx. 225MB). The test consistently reports Memory PSI and passes.

PSI metrics were not emitted when memory.high was set to max (default) and memory.max was set to 200/250MB. This is expected, as memory pressure is primarily felt and reported when usage is constrained between the memory.high (soft) and memory.max (hard) limits.

Yet to work on the changes required

comments.author: haircommander
comments.body:
I do wonder if relying on memoryQoS is a good idea, as it's an alpha feature and we haven't gained consensus upstream that it's the correct direction (or rather, without PSI metrics being used to verify we're not in a livelock situation, which would require a new kep probably?)

 Are we setting memory overcommit on these nodes? you can get memory usage above the memory limit if so, and I imagine pressure would be felt in that scenario?

comments.author: mariafromano-25
comments.body: Since memoryQoS is still in alpha, as an alternative, is there a way to have a workload that can directly set the memory.high similar to this scenario so it can reliably generate the memory pressure?

comments.author: haircommander
comments.body: setting memory.high without a way to detect livelock is risky though. basically, as a memory hungry container approaches memory.high, the kernel aggressively reclaims that memory. If the container continually allocates however, that means that memory usage is effectively locked with no path towards being killed. I think a goal of PSI could be using memory pressure to also influence evictions, so if the kubelet detects a container is aggressively allocating memory but not getting killed it could be evicted, but that requires PSI metrics be accurately tested, which creates a cyclical dependency :\

comments.author: roycaihw
comments.body:
The current PSI test focus on the metrics surfacing. Setting a static memory.high doesn't represent real-world use case but is a reliable way to generate memory pressure, which allows the test to verify the surfacing behavior. Can we use a static memory.high to stablize the current test? 

I agree that a real-world usage of memory.high is more dynamic. Also agree on using testing and developing PSI-based eviction. But they are separate features and not the focus of this flaky test.

comments.author: haircommander
comments.body: who do you want to set static memory.high? the kubelet? I'd be opposed to that, but you could potentially set it manually by finding the container cgroup.

comments.author: ngopalak-redhat
comments.body:
@roycaihw / @haircommander An update:

I did some testing using the approach of mounting the cgroup path within a privileged pod. I've observed that the container runtime (most probably) is resetting the `memory.high` value inside `/sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice` to the max.

Draft PR: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134064/files

I found a way to set `memory.high` in kubepods-burstable.slice and all its subfolders during the test, which successfully generated the memory pressure PSI metrics:

```
"sleep 10; i=0; while true; do find /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice -type f -name \"memory.high\" -exec sh -c 'echo \"195103808\" | tee {} > /dev/null' \\;; dd if=/dev/zero of=testfile.$i bs=1M count=50 &>/dev/null; i=$(((i+1)%9)); sleep 0.1; done"
```

I had successful runs locally and one successful CI run as well (see the links: https://testgrid.k8s.io/sig-node-cri-o#pr-node-kubelet-serial-crio-cgroupv2&width=90 or https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/directory/pull-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-crio-cgroupv2/1975492483198488576).

I also had to make the difference between `memory.high` and `memory.max` quite large. When `memory.high` was 80% of `memory.max`, the results were flaky on Fedora.

The next step is to set `/sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/memory.high` only (I mean not in the sub-folders) and verify that it's used, even if the pod and container cgroups under that directory use the max for memory.high. According to the documentation, this should work. I also need to implement cleanup after the test.

thread_text:
ISSUE #134063: CVE-2025-9708: Kubernetes C# Client: improper certificate validation in custom CA mode may lead to man-in-the-middle attacks
Author: ritazh
Date: 2025-09-15T04:59:12Z
Labels: kind/bug, area/security, committee/security-response, triage/accepted, official-cve-feed
State: closed

[c0]
**CVSS Rating:**  
[CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3-1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) — **Medium (6.8)**


A vulnerability exists in the Kubernetes C# client where the certificate validation logic accepts properly constructed certificates from any Certificate Authority (CA) without properly verifying the trust chain. This flaw allows a malicious actor to present a forged certificate and potentially intercept or manipulate communication with the Kubernetes API server, leading to possible man-in-the-middle attacks and API impersonation.

### Am I vulnerable?

You are vulnerable if:
- You use the Kubernetes C# client to connect to a Kubernetes API server over TLS/HTTPS  with custom CA certificates in your kubeconfig file and your connection occurs over an untrusted network.

#### Affected Versions
- All versions of the Kubernetes C# client prior to the next release <=17.0.13

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

This issue can be mitigated by:
- Deploy the patch version of the Kubernetes C# client as soon as possible.
- Moving the CA certificates into the system trust store instead of specifying them in the kubeconfig file. Note: This approach may introduce new risks, as all processes on the system will begin to trust certificates signed by that CA. If you must use an affected version, you can disable custom CA and add the CA to the machine's trusted root.


#### Fixed Versions

- Kubernetes C# client >= v17.0.14

### Detection

To determine if your applications are affected:
- Review your usage of the Kubernetes C# client and inspect certificate validation logic.
- Review your kubeconfig files and determine if you use a custom CA certificate (the certificate-authority field in the clusters section).
- Review client logs for unexpected or untrusted certificate connections.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by @elliott-beach

The issue was fixed and coordinated by: 

Boshi Lian @tg123
Brendan Burns @brendandburns
Rita Zhang @ritazh
